Here, we quantify how large dams impact the presence of fish species along the river
continuum in four french watersheds (Loire, Somme, Seine, Gironde).

## Summary

We find that

- dams accumulate with altitude, so their effect is confounded with the position along the river
- 6 of 48 species are credibly less frequent above dams: the eel, brackish-tolerant species and the wels catfish
- the spatial field absorbs part of the dam effect: without it, three times more species respond
- the spatial fields share a cold-water vs warm-water axis that follows summer temperature

```{r setup}
renv::load()
library(targets)
library(here)
tar_config_set(

)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

nice_theme()
```

## Preparing dam dataset

### Keeping large dams

```{r roe-count}
basin_kept <- tar_read(basin) |>
  filter(district %in% tar_read(params)$district_kept)
roe_kept <- tar_read(roe) |>
  sf::st_filter(sf::st_transform(basin_kept, sf::st_crs(tar_read(roe)))) |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry()
dam_weir_unknown_n <- roe_kept |>
  filter(
    grepl("barrage|seuil", LbTypeOuvrage, ignore.case = TRUE),
    !CdHautChutClObstEcoul %in% as.character(1:8)
  ) |>
  nrow()
large_dam_evidence <- tar_read(large_dam) |>
  sf::st_filter(sf::st_transform(basin_kept, sf::st_crs(tar_read(large_dam)))) |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  count(evidence)
evidence_n <- setNames(large_dam_evidence$n, large_dam_evidence$evidence)
large_dam_n <- sum(evidence_n)
```

We use the ROE database from OFB. The database lists artificial obstacles in
French rivers. We keep dams and weirs with a drop height of 5 meters or more.
We keep four dams marked as destroyed they were removed at the very end of our
sampling or after.

The drop height class is missing for many obstacles, some large dam may be among
them.

Obstacles only matter here if they lie on the river network with sampled
sites upstream of them. Each obstacle is snapped on the network with a threshold
of 100 m.

```{r drop-height-missing}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| cache: true

district_label <- c(
  "Ardour-Garonne" = "Adour-Garonne", "Escaut-Somme" = "Escaut-Somme",
  "Loire" = "Loire", "Seine" = "Seine"
)
dam_network <- tar_read(dam_network)$network
river_edge <- sf::st_as_sf(tar_read(river_network_geo)$edges)
obstacle <- tar_read(roe) |>
  sf::st_join(
    sf::st_transform(select(basin_kept, district), sf::st_crs(tar_read(roe))),
    join = sf::st_within, left = FALSE
  ) |>
  sf::st_transform(sf::st_crs(river_edge)) |>
  transmute(
    roe_code = CdObstEcoul,
    district = district_label[district],
    kind = if_else(grepl("seuil", LbTypeOuvrage, ignore.case = TRUE), "weir", "dam"),
    drop_class = if_else(CdHautChutClObstEcoul %in% as.character(1:8), "known", "missing"),
    group = case_when(
      !LbEtOuvrage %in% c("Existant", "Détruit entièrement", "Détruit partiellement") ~ "planned or no status",
      !grepl("barrage|seuil", LbTypeOuvrage, ignore.case = TRUE) ~ "other type",
      roe_code %in% tar_read(large_dam)$roe_code ~ "large (kept)",
      CdHautChutClObstEcoul %in% as.character(1:6) ~ "small (< 5 m)",
      TRUE ~ "unknown size"
    )
  )
dam_weir <- filter(obstacle, group %in% c("large (kept)", "small (< 5 m)", "unknown size"))
dam_weir$snap_dist_m <- as.numeric(sf::st_distance(
  dam_weir, river_edge[sf::st_nearest_feature(dam_weir, river_edge), ], by_element = TRUE
))
dam_weir_on <- filter(dam_weir, snap_dist_m <= 100)
network_node <- sf::st_as_sf(dam_network$nodes)
dam_weir_on$node_id <- network_node$node_id[sf::st_nearest_feature(dam_weir_on, network_node)]
dam_weir_visit <- locate_operations_dams(
  dam_network,
  tar_read(inland_operations_snapped) |> filter(survey == "river"),
  dam_weir_on,
  tar_read(river_mouth_district)
) |>
  filter(position == "upstream", operation_id %in% tar_read(dam_visit)$operation_id) |>
  distinct(roe_code)
dam_weir <- dam_weir |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  mutate(
    position = case_when(
      snap_dist_m > 100 ~ "too far from the network (> 100 m)",
      roe_code %in% dam_weir_visit$roe_code ~ "on the network, sites upstream",
      TRUE ~ "on the network, no site upstream"
    )
  )
dam_weir_relevant <- filter(dam_weir, position == "on the network, sites upstream")
dam_weir_relevant |>
  count(district, kind, drop_class) |>
  ggplot(aes(district, n, fill = drop_class)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~kind, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(known = "#4A90C2", missing = "grey70")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Obstacles", fill = "Drop height\nclass") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))
```

Dams and weirs on the network with sampled sites upstream, with a known
or missing drop height class.

For the obstacles of unknown class, the drop height is inferred from the
structure height, when it is available. Drop height raises with obstacle height.

From available data, we use the following thresholds:

1. A dam of 7.5 m or more is set to a drop of 5 m or more
2. A dam of 15 m or more is set to a drop of 10 m or more

```{r drop-height-calibration}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.5

tar_read(roe) |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(
    LbEtOuvrage == "Existant",
    grepl("barrage", LbTypeOuvrage, ignore.case = TRUE),
    CdHautChutClObstEcoul %in% as.character(1:8)
  ) |>
  mutate(structure_height = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(HautMaxTer))) |>
  filter(structure_height > 0) |>
  mutate(band = cut(structure_height, c(0, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7.5, 10, 12.5, 15, 20, 30, 50, Inf), right = FALSE)) |>
  summarise(
    height = median(structure_height), dams = n(),
    `5 m or more` = mean(CdHautChutClObstEcoul %in% c("7", "8")),
    `10 m or more` = mean(CdHautChutClObstEcoul == "8"),
    .by = band
  ) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(`5 m or more`, `10 m or more`), names_to = "drop", values_to = "share") |>
  mutate(drop = factor(drop, c("5 m or more", "10 m or more"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(height, share, color = drop)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(7.5, 15), linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.9, linetype = "dotted", color = "grey50") +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(aes(size = dams)) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(1, 2, 5, 7.5, 15, 30, 100)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#E69F00", "#B2182B")) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 4) +
  labs(x = "Structure height (m)", y = "Share of dams", color = "Drop height", size = "Dams")
```


The measured drop height and the structure height of weirs are not used:
they hold impossible values (weirs of tens to hundreds of meters, often their
length).

Large dams whose drop height class and structure height are both missing are
left out: we may miss some, but we assume that we keep most of them.

This leaves us with `r format(large_dam_n, big.mark = ",")` obstacles
(hereafter "dams" for simplicity): `r format(evidence_n[["class"]], big.mark = ",")`
from their drop height class and `r evidence_n[["structure height"]]` from
their structure height. The table below gives why the other obstacles are
left out.

```{r left-out-reason}
options(knitr.kable.NA = "")
bind_rows(
  sf::st_drop_geometry(obstacle) |>
    filter(!group %in% dam_weir$group) |>
    count(group, name = "total"),
  dam_weir |>
    count(group, kind, position) |>
    tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = position, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
    mutate(total = rowSums(across(where(is.numeric))))
) |>
  mutate(group = factor(group, c(
    "large (kept)", "small (< 5 m)", "unknown size",
    "other type", "planned or no status"
  ))) |>
  arrange(group, kind) |>
  select(
    group, kind, total, `too far from the network (> 100 m)`,
    `on the network, no site upstream`, `on the network, sites upstream`
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

Here is the number of obstacles per catchment, height and kind.

```{r large-dam-district}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.5

district_label <- c(
  "Ardour-Garonne" = "Adour-Garonne", "Escaut-Somme" = "Escaut-Somme",
  "Loire" = "Loire", "Seine" = "Seine"
)
dam_with_site <- tar_read(operation_dam) |>
  filter(position == "upstream", operation_id %in% tar_read(dam_visit)$operation_id) |>
  distinct(roe_code)
large_dam_district <- tar_read(large_dam) |>
  semi_join(dam_with_site, by = "roe_code") |>
  sf::st_join(
    tar_read(basin) |>
      filter(district %in% tar_read(params)$district_kept) |>
      sf::st_transform(sf::st_crs(tar_read(large_dam))) |>
      select(district),
    join = sf::st_within, left = FALSE
  ) |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  mutate(
    district = district_label[district],
    drop_height = factor(drop_height_min, c(5, 10), c("5-10 m", ">= 10 m"))
  )
large_dam_district |>
  count(district, kind, drop_height) |>
  ggplot(aes(district, n, fill = drop_height)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~kind, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#E69F00", "#B2182B")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Obstacles", fill = "Drop height") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))
```

### Placing the dams on the river network

The dams between a site and the sea are counted along the river
network. Each dam is placed on the network from its own ROE coordinates,
in four steps:

1. **Snapping.** The dam is placed on the nearest river segment, if it is
   within 100 m of the ROE coordinates.
2. **River name.** When a segment bearing the ROE river name lies within
   100 m, it is preferred to a nearer segment of another river.
3. **Close dams.** Dams less than 1 km apart on the same flow path count
   as one. They act as one barrier for fish moving along the river (and are
   often two ROE codes of one structure, such as a weir and its power
   plant). Going up from the sea, a dam is merged into the nearest kept
   dam downstream if it lies within 1 km of it.
4. **Routing.** The dams of a site are those on its route to the sea, the
   shortest path through the network to the river mouth, which also gives the
   distance to the mouth. We penalize artificial canals such that they count 100 times
   their length for the choice of the route only. We do so because sometimes the
   shortest path to the sea was going through them, masking the dams of the natural
   riverbed or adding dams of the canal.

Here is the table of the dams that are snapped from distance, snapped using
river name, merged (if close), and eventually left out.

```{r large-dam}
large_dam <- tar_read(large_dam)
basin_kept <- tar_read(basin) |>
  filter(district %in% tar_read(params)$district_kept) |>
  sf::st_transform(sf::st_crs(large_dam))
large_dam_kept <- large_dam |>
  sf::st_filter(basin_kept) |>
  mutate(
    drop_height = factor(drop_height_min, c(5, 10), c("5-10 m", ">= 10 m")),
    match = factor(coalesce(match, "left out"), c("nearest", "name", "merged", "left out"))
  )
placement <- sf::st_drop_geometry(large_dam_kept) |>
  mutate(placed = match %in% c("nearest", "name"))
placed_dist <- placement$snap_dist_m[placement$placed]
left_far <- filter(placement, match == "left out")
sf::st_drop_geometry(large_dam_kept) |>
  count(kind, match) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = match, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)
```

And here is the distribution of the snapping distance for the dams that are
kept.

```{r large-dam-match-plot}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3

large_dam_kept |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(match %in% c("nearest", "name")) |>
  mutate(
    match = factor(match, c("nearest", "name"), c("nearest segment", "segment with its river name"))
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(pmax(snap_dist_m, 0.1))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40) +
  facet_wrap(~match, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_number()) +
  labs(x = "Distance between the dam and its segment (m)", y = "Dams")
```

The other `r nrow(left_far)` dams
(`r round(100 * nrow(left_far) / nrow(placement))`%) are left out because
they lie more than 100 m from any river segment (median `r round(median(left_far$snap_dist_m), -1)` m),
mostly pond and reservoir embankments on small streams the network does
not include. To check that leaving
them out does not matter, each was placed on its nearest network node and
the visits upstream of it were counted.

```{r left-out-dam}
dam_network <- tar_read(dam_network)$network
network_node <- sf::st_as_sf(dam_network$nodes)
left_out <- large_dam_kept |>
  filter(match == "left out") |>
  sf::st_transform(sf::st_crs(network_node))
left_out$node_id <- network_node$node_id[sf::st_nearest_feature(left_out, network_node)]
left_out_visit <- locate_operations_dams(
  dam_network,
  tar_read(inland_operations_snapped) |> filter(survey == "river"),
  left_out,
  tar_read(river_mouth_district)
) |>
  filter(position == "upstream", operation_id %in% tar_read(dam_visit)$operation_id) |>
  count(roe_code, name = "visits_upstream")
left_out_upstream <- left_out |>
  sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
  inner_join(left_out_visit, by = "roe_code")
left_out_upstream |>
  transmute(roe_code, name, type, distance_m = round(snap_dist_m), visits_upstream) |>
  arrange(desc(visits_upstream)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Only `r nrow(left_out_upstream)` of the `r nrow(left_far)`
dams left out for their distance would have sampled visits upstream
(`r sum(left_out_upstream$visits_upstream)` visits in all), and these lie
`r round(min(left_out_upstream$snap_dist_m), -1)` to
`r round(max(left_out_upstream$snap_dist_m), -1)` m from the network, mostly
pond dams: placing them on the nearest node would
put them on the river next to the pond, where they do not stand. The
left-out dams therefore do not change the dam counts of the sites.

Large dams on the network with sampled sites upstream (those that enter the
dam counts of the sites), by drop height class and kind, on the RHT rivers
of Strahler order 3 or more.

```{r large-dam-map}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 10

rht <- tar_read(rht)
river_line <- rht |>
  filter(strahler >= 3) |>
  sf::st_transform(sf::st_crs(large_dam)) |>
  sf::st_filter(basin_kept)
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = basin_kept, fill = "grey97", color = "grey40") +
  geom_sf(data = river_line, aes(linewidth = strahler), color = "#4A90C2") +
  geom_sf(
    data = large_dam_kept |> semi_join(dam_with_site, by = "roe_code") |> arrange(drop_height_min),
    aes(color = drop_height, shape = kind), size = 2
  ) +
  scale_linewidth(range = c(0.1, 1), guide = "none") +
  scale_shape_manual(name = "Obstacle", values = c(dam = 16, weir = 17)) +
  scale_color_manual(name = "Drop height", values = c("#E69F00", "#B2182B")) +
  theme_void()
```

### How dams accumulate along the river network

An operation is upstream of a dam if the dam lies on its path to the mouth, and
downstream if it lies on the dam's path to the mouth (`operation_dam`, river
operations).

```{r operation-dam}
operation_dam <- tar_read(operation_dam) |>
  left_join(
    tar_read(river_operation) |> distinct(operation_id, sandre_code),
    by = "operation_id"
  ) |>
  left_join(
    large_dam |> sf::st_drop_geometry() |> select(roe_code, kind, drop_height_min),
    by = "roe_code"
  )
river_ops <- tar_read(inland_operations_snapped) |>
  filter(survey == "river") |>
  left_join(
    tar_read(inland_distance_to_mouth) |> select(operation_id, dist_mouth_m),
    by = "operation_id"
  )

dam_below <- operation_dam |>
  filter(position == "upstream") |>
  count(operation_id, name = "dams")
river_ops <- river_ops |>
  left_join(dam_below, by = "operation_id") |>
  mutate(dams = coalesce(dams, 0L))

river_ops |>
  summarise(operations = n(), with_dam_below = mean(dams > 0))
```

Number of large dams between each operation and the sea.

```{r dam-maps}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 7

river_ops |>
  ggplot(aes(longitude, latitude, color = pmin(dams, 5))) +
  geom_sf(
    data = sf::st_transform(basin_kept, 4326), fill = "grey97",
    color = "grey40", inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_point(size = 0.6) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(name = "Number of dams\ndownstream", labels = c(0:4, "5+")) +
  theme_void()
```

```{r dams-vs-distance-mouth}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.5

ggplot(river_ops, aes(dist_mouth_m / 1000, dams)) +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.1, size = 0.5, alpha = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~district) +
  labs(x = "Distance to the mouth (km)", y = "Number of dams downstream")
```

## A case study with Mervent and Tuilières dams

Before modelling France, we look at two specific dams: Mervent (Vendée) and
Tuilières (Dordogne). Mervent is the first large dam from the sea on the Vendée.
Tuilières is the first large dam on the Dordogne. We compare fishing operations
within 100km upstream and dowstream of each dam (same flow path).

```{r case-study-sites}
focus_dam <- c(Mervent = "ROE39720", Tuilieres = "ROE66029")
migratory <- c(
  "Anguilla anguilla", "Salmo salar", "Petromyzon marinus",
  "Lampetra fluviatilis", "Platichthys flesus", "Chelon ramada", "Chelon auratus"
)
river_effort <- tar_read(river_effort)

focus_operation <- operation_dam |>
  filter(roe_code %in% focus_dam, river_dist_m <= 100000) |>
  mutate(dam = names(focus_dam)[match(roe_code, focus_dam)]) |>
  left_join(river_effort, by = "operation_id")
```

Occurrence of each species downstream and upstream of each dam, for the
operations with individual fish records: the share of visits where it is caught
at each site, averaged over the sites (each site weighs the same, however often
it was visited). The effect of the dam is summarised by the difference in
occurrence (upstream minus downstream; negative: less frequent upstream).

```{r case-study-presence}
focus_presence <- tar_read(river_size) |>
  mutate(operation_id = as.character(operation_id)) |>
  semi_join(focus_operation, by = "operation_id") |>
  distinct(operation_id, species_valid)

focus_species <- focus_operation |>
  filter(has_individuals) |>
  tidyr::crossing(species_valid = unique(focus_presence$species_valid)) |>
  left_join(
    focus_presence |> mutate(present = TRUE),
    by = c("operation_id", "species_valid")
  ) |>
  summarise(
    occurrence = mean(coalesce(present, FALSE)),
    .by = c(dam, species_valid, position, sandre_code)
  ) |>
  summarise(occurrence = mean(occurrence), .by = c(dam, species_valid, position)) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(
    names_from = position, values_from = occurrence, names_prefix = "occurrence_"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    difference = occurrence_upstream - occurrence_downstream,
    migratory = species_valid %in% migratory
  )

focus_operation |>
  filter(has_individuals) |>
  summarise(operations = n(), sites = n_distinct(sandre_code), .by = c(dam, position))
```

```{r case-study-difference-plot}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 9

difference_plot <- function(dam_name) {
  focus_species |>
    filter(dam == dam_name) |>
    mutate(species_valid = reorder(species_valid, difference)) |>
    ggplot(aes(difference, species_valid, color = migratory)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
    geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = difference, yend = species_valid)) +
    geom_point() +
    scale_color_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey40", `TRUE` = "#B2182B")) +
    labs(
      title = dam_name, x = "Occurrence upstream - occurrence downstream",
      y = NULL, color = "Migratory"
    ) +
    theme(axis.text.y = element_text(face = "italic"))
}
patchwork::wrap_plots(lapply(names(focus_dam), difference_plot), guides = "collect")
```

Upstream of dams species that migrate from the sea (e.g. eels) decreases. Dams
slow down their migration further upstream in the river. This is the main
expected impact of dams.

## Presence models

### Measuring dam impact

We focus on the impact of dams preventing fish migration. To capture this effect
we use the number of dam downstream of a site. This captures the barrier effect
between the site and the sea. An important thing to have in mind is that
accumulation of dams increases as we go upstream (see below).

```{r visits}
# Visits and presences shared with the presence models (targets `dam_visit`,
# `river_presence`): position controls centred, dams = large dams + large
# weirs between the site and the sea.
continuum_operation <- tar_read(continuum_operation)
presence <- tar_read(river_presence)
visit <- tar_read(dam_visit)
c(
  visits = nrow(visit), sites = n_distinct(visit$sandre_code),
  catchments = n_distinct(visit$catchment)
)
```

Number of large dams and large weirs between each site and the sea against
the altitude and the distance to the mouth (one point per site).

```{r visits-dams-plot}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 7

visit_site <- distinct(visit, sandre_code, .keep_all = TRUE)
visit_site |>
  transmute(
    sandre_code, dam_count, weir_count, dams,
    altitude = exp(log_altitude), distance = dist_mouth_m / 1000
  ) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(dam_count, weir_count, dams), names_to = "obstacle", values_to = "count") |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(altitude, distance), names_to = "axis", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(
    obstacle = factor(obstacle, c("dam_count", "weir_count", "dams"), c("Dams", "Weirs", "Total (dams + weirs)")),
    axis = factor(axis, c("altitude", "distance"), c("Altitude (m)", "Distance to the mouth (km)"))
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(value, count)) +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.15, width = 0, size = 0.4, alpha = 0.3) +
  facet_grid(obstacle ~ axis, scales = "free_x", switch = "x") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_number()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Large obstacles downstream") +
  theme(strip.placement = "outside")
```

Weirs matter and can be large. Obstacles accumulate with altitude, much
more than with the distance to the mouth: almost all mountain sites have
several large dams or weirs downstream.

### Designing the model

Next, we model the impact downstream dam accumulation on species presence. When
designing our model we have to be careful to include enough environment
variables such that model can disentangle the effect of environments and dams.
These effects are correlated if we for example consider elevation. We have also
to ensure that the model is identifiable. Many environmental covariables are
correlated such that including too many of them may harm the model. To ensure
this doesn't happen we check the variance inflation factor (VIF) of each model
term. VIF enables to quantify the collinearity of each term with others, which
informs on how adding this term to the model inflates the model uncertainty. VIF
below 5 indicates low to moderate collinearity and is generally acceptable. VIF
higher than 10 indicates severe collinearity making the model non-identifiable
[@Dormann-etal-2013].

Once the models are designed, we will also investigate posterior correlations to
ensure that the model is able to disentangle covariable effects.

Here is the list of our fixed effect candidates:

- dam impacts (included by default)
- river width
- altitude
- distance to river mouth
- slope
- strahler order

Below we plot their pairwise correlations (Spearman) and their VIF, so we can
better decide which one to include.

```{r position-identifiability}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.5

position_variable <- visit |>
  left_join(continuum_operation |> select(operation_id, strahler), by = "operation_id") |>
  transmute(
    `log(1 + dams)` = log1p(dams), `log width` = log_width, `log altitude` = log_alt,
    `log distance to the mouth` = log_dist, `log slope` = log_slope, `Strahler order` = strahler
  )
position_correlation <- cor(position_variable, method = "spearman")
correlation_plot <- as_tibble(position_correlation, rownames = "x") |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-x, names_to = "y", values_to = "rho") |>
  mutate(
    x = factor(x, colnames(position_correlation)),
    y = factor(y, rev(colnames(position_correlation)))
  ) |>
  filter(as.integer(x) < ncol(position_correlation) + 1 - as.integer(y)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y, fill = rho)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", rho)), size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166AC", high = "#B2182B", limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Spearman\ncorrelation") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1), panel.grid = element_blank())
vif <- function(term) {
  sapply(term, \(k) {
    1 / (1 - summary(lm(reformulate(sprintf("`%s`", setdiff(term, k)), sprintf("`%s`", k)), position_variable))$r.squared)
  })
}
candidate_term <- colnames(position_variable)
reduced_term <- setdiff(candidate_term, "Strahler order")
position_vif <- bind_rows(
  tibble(term = candidate_term, vif = vif(candidate_term), set = "all candidates"),
  tibble(term = reduced_term, vif = vif(reduced_term), set = "without the Strahler order")
)
vif_plot <- position_vif |>
  filter(term != "Strahler order") |>
  mutate(term = factor(term, rev(candidate_term))) |>
  ggplot(aes(vif, term, fill = set)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(preserve = "single")) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 5, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#E69F00", "grey40")) +
  labs(x = "Variance inflation factor", y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
patchwork::wrap_plots(correlation_plot, vif_plot, widths = c(1.2, 1)) +
  patchwork::plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")
```

Strahler order and river width tells the same thing: they are strongly
correlated, and including both raise the VIF beyond 5. We'll go for river width
only. All other variables can be safely included, as they are not too strongly
correlated, and their VIF lies safely below 5.

### Fitting the first model

We test a first model that include all these covariables (linear), and the
following random effects:

- year
- site
- spatial random field to handle spatial autocorrelation

A catchment effect was also tried, but its variance was estimated at
almost zero for both species (about $10^{-4}$, against 2.3 for the site
effect of the gudgeon): once the spatial field is in, the catchments add
nothing, so it is left out.

To begin with we need to generate a mesh for the spatial random field.

```{r spatial-mesh}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 7

# Spatial random field of the presence models: SPDE mesh over the sites
# (Lambert-93, km, target `presence_mesh`) and projection of the field at
# the visits.
site_xy <- visit_coordinates(visit)
spatial_mesh <- tar_read(presence_mesh)
spatial_A <- INLA::inla.spde.make.A(spatial_mesh, loc = site_xy)
mesh_box <- sf::st_bbox(c(
  xmin = min(spatial_mesh$loc[, 1]), xmax = max(spatial_mesh$loc[, 1]),
  ymin = min(spatial_mesh$loc[, 2]), ymax = max(spatial_mesh$loc[, 2])
) * 1000, crs = sf::st_crs(2154))
coast <- coastline() |>
  sf::st_crop(sf::st_bbox(sf::st_transform(sf::st_as_sfc(mesh_box), 4326))) |>
  sf::st_transform(2154) |>
  sf::st_geometry()
plot(spatial_mesh, main = "", asp = 1, col = "grey")
plot(coast / 1000, add = TRUE, col = "black", lwd = 1.5)
points(unique(site_xy), pch = 16, cex = 0.3, col = "blue")
```

We fit the model on three species:

- the gudgeon *Gobio gobio* (*goujon*) found in most french rivers
- the brown trout *Salmo trutta* (*truite*), an upland species
- the bream *Abramis brama* (*brème*), a lowland species

We show below the effects of the model for these three species.

```{r first-model}
#| cache: true
#| cache.extra: !expr rlang::hash(list(visit, presence, spatial_mesh, deparse(fit_presence_model)))

# Presence model of `species` on `term` (dam and position terms) + effort
# + site and year effects + spatial field: `fit_presence_model()`, also used
# by the targets of all species.
first_coefficient <- purrr::map_dfr(c("Gobio gobio", "Salmo trutta", "Abramis brama"), function(species) {
  model <- fit_presence_model(
    visit, presence, spatial_mesh, species,
    "accumulation + log_width + log_alt + log_dist + log_slope"
  )
  as_tibble(model$summary.fixed, rownames = "term") |>
    transmute(
      species, term, estimate = mean, lower = `0.025quant`, upper = `0.975quant`
    )
})
```

```{r first-model-plot}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 3.5

position_label <- c(
  accumulation = "log(1 + dams)", log_width = "log width", log_alt = "log altitude",
  log_dist = "log distance to the mouth", log_slope = "log slope"
)
first_coefficient |>
  filter(term %in% names(position_label)) |>
  mutate(
    term = factor(position_label[term], rev(position_label)),
    species = factor(species, c("Gobio gobio", "Salmo trutta", "Abramis brama"))
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(estimate, term)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper), size = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~species, nrow = 1) +
  labs(x = "Effect on the logit scale", y = NULL) +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "italic"))
```

We retrieve that altitude has a positive effect on the brown trout and a
negative one the bream. We also see a clear positive effect of the distance on
the trout, to see what this effect capture we plot the residuals (predicted
probability of presence vs observed) map including or not the distance effect.

::: {.callout-note}
We do not include the spatial field in the prediction as it can captures
patterns missed by covariates and make the residuals appear better than what is
truly captured by the covariates.
:::

```{r distance-models}
#| cache: true
#| cache.extra: !expr rlang::hash(list(visit, presence, spatial_mesh, deparse(fit_presence_model)))

map_species <- c("Gobio gobio", "Salmo trutta", "Abramis brama")
distance_term <- c(
  `with distance` = "accumulation + log_width + log_alt + log_dist + log_slope",
  `without distance` = "accumulation + log_width + log_alt + log_slope"
)

# Presence probability at each site predicted by `model` without the local
# variations of the spatial field (field at its mean over the visits),
# averaged over the site effect distribution (50 quantiles of a normal with
# the estimated site variance), then over the visits of the site.
site_probability <- function(model) {
  eta <- model$summary.linear.predictor$mean[seq_len(nrow(visit))]
  field <- as.vector(spatial_A %*% model$summary.random$spatial$mean)
  site_effect <- model$summary.random$site$mean[match(visit$site, model$summary.random$site$ID)]
  site_sd <- 1 / sqrt(model$summary.hyperpar["Precision for site", "mean"])
  covariate_part <- eta - site_effect - field + mean(field)
  visit |>
    mutate(p = rowMeans(plogis(outer(covariate_part, site_sd * qnorm(ppoints(50)), `+`)))) |>
    summarise(p = mean(p), n = n(), .by = sandre_code)
}
species_fit <- tidyr::expand_grid(species = map_species, model = names(distance_term)) |>
  mutate(fit = purrr::map2(species, model, function(s, m) {
    model <- fit_presence_model(visit, presence, spatial_mesh, s, distance_term[[m]])
    list(prediction = site_probability(model), field = model$summary.random$spatial$mean)
  }))
species_prediction <- species_fit |>
  mutate(prediction = purrr::map(fit, "prediction")) |>
  select(-fit) |>
  tidyr::unnest(prediction)
# Spatial field of the models with distance, at the mesh nodes.
species_field <- species_fit |>
  filter(model == "with distance") |>
  transmute(species, field = purrr::map(fit, "field"))
```


Share of the visits of each site where the species was caught (grey: never
caught).

```{r species-map}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.5

# Observed share of the visits of each site where each species was caught.
species_site <- purrr::map_dfr(map_species, function(species) {
  visit |>
    mutate(present = operation_id %in% presence$operation_id[presence$species_valid == species]) |>
    summarise(
      observed = mean(present), longitude = first(longitude), latitude = first(latitude),
      .by = sandre_code
    ) |>
    mutate(species = species)
}) |>
  mutate(species = factor(species, map_species))

ggplot(species_site, aes(longitude, latitude)) +
  geom_sf(
    data = sf::st_transform(basin_kept, 4326), fill = "grey97",
    color = "grey40", inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_point(data = filter(species_site, observed == 0), color = "grey75", size = 0.3) +
  geom_point(
    data = filter(species_site, observed > 0) |> arrange(observed),
    aes(color = observed), size = 0.6
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~species) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(name = "Share of visits", limits = c(0, 1)) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "italic", size = 11))
```

```{r species-residual-map}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.5

# Hexagons of 40 km over the sites (Lambert-93).
site_hexagon <- distinct(species_site, sandre_code, longitude, latitude) |>
  sf::st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326) |>
  sf::st_transform(2154)
hexagon <- sf::st_make_grid(site_hexagon, cellsize = 40000, square = FALSE) |>
  sf::st_as_sf() |>
  mutate(hexagon = row_number())
site_hexagon <- tibble(
  sandre_code = site_hexagon$sandre_code,
  hexagon = sapply(sf::st_intersects(site_hexagon, hexagon), `[`, 1)
)

# Predicted minus observed presence of `prediction` (one row per site and
# model, with `p` and the number of visits `n`), averaged over the visits
# in each hexagon.
residual_hexagon <- function(prediction, ...) {
  prediction |>
    inner_join(species_site, by = c("species", "sandre_code")) |>
    inner_join(site_hexagon, by = "sandre_code") |>
    summarise(residual = weighted.mean(p - observed, n), .by = c(hexagon, ...)) |>
    inner_join(hexagon, x = _, by = "hexagon") |>
    sf::st_as_sf()
}
residual_scale <- scale_fill_distiller(
  palette = "RdBu", limits = c(-0.6, 0.6), oob = scales::squish,
  name = "Predicted minus\nobserved presence"
)

species_prediction |>
  mutate(species = factor(species, map_species)) |>
  filter(species == "Salmo trutta") |>
  residual_hexagon(species, model) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = residual), color = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = sf::st_transform(basin_kept, 2154), fill = NA, color = "grey40") +
  facet_wrap(~model) +
  residual_scale +
  theme_void() +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 11))

```

For the brown trout the negative distance effect captures the absence of the
species in western Brittany.

### Evaluating the first model

To evaluate how the model performs and how it functions we can have a look at
the spatial field. The spatial field can capture effect of missing covariates or
capture true biogeographical effect. By investigating its patterns, we can
understand what the model captures and misses. We plot the spatial random field
for our three species.

```{r species-field-map}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.5

# 5 km grid (Lambert-93, km) over the basins, projected from the mesh.
basin_union <- sf::st_union(sf::st_transform(basin_kept, 2154))
field_grid <- sf::st_make_grid(basin_union, cellsize = 5000, what = "centers")
field_grid <- sf::st_coordinates(field_grid[lengths(sf::st_intersects(field_grid, basin_union)) > 0])
field_A <- INLA::inla.spde.make.A(spatial_mesh, loc = field_grid / 1000)
field_map <- species_field |>
  mutate(value = purrr::map(field, function(field) {
    tibble(
      x = field_grid[, "X"], y = field_grid[, "Y"],
      value = as.vector(field_A %*% field) - mean(as.vector(spatial_A %*% field))
    )
  })) |>
  select(-field) |>
  tidyr::unnest(value) |>
  mutate(species = factor(species, map_species))
field_limit <- max(abs(field_map$value))
ggplot(field_map) +
  geom_raster(aes(x, y, fill = value)) +
  geom_sf(data = sf::st_transform(basin_kept, 2154), fill = NA, color = "grey40") +
  facet_wrap(~species) +
  scale_fill_distiller(
    palette = "PuOr", direction = 1, limits = c(-field_limit, field_limit),
    name = "Spatial field\n(logit)"
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "italic", size = 11))
```

Field capture regional patterns for the bream and the brown trout potentially
reflecting dispersal history, connection large rivers, etc. For the gudgeon, the
field seems to reflect part of remaining altitude effect, as it takes negative
values at high altitude. To check for that we add a quadratic term to the model
and see how it changes its performance by looking at its WAIC and residuals in
space.

### Linear or quadratic altitude?

We fit a model for the gudgeon with a quadratic altitude term and compare its
residuals with the previous model, as well as its WAIC, to see if it performs
any better. We also have a look at how this adding this control changes the dam
effect, as this ultimately what we want to capture, and so remove any bias that
can affect it.

```{r altitude-shape-models}
#| cache: true
#| cache.extra: !expr rlang::hash(list(visit, presence, spatial_mesh, deparse(fit_presence_model), deparse(site_probability)))

altitude_term <- c(
  linear = "accumulation + log_width + log_alt + log_dist + log_slope",
  quadratic = "accumulation + log_width + log_alt + I(log_alt^2) + log_dist + log_slope"
)
altitude_model <- lapply(
  altitude_term, \(term) fit_presence_model(visit, presence, spatial_mesh, "Gobio gobio", term)
)
altitude_fit <- purrr::imap_dfr(altitude_model, \(m, shape) tibble(
  shape,
  dam_effect = sprintf(
    "%.2f (%.2f, %.2f)", m$summary.fixed["accumulation", "mean"],
    m$summary.fixed["accumulation", "0.025quant"], m$summary.fixed["accumulation", "0.975quant"]
  ),
  waic = m$waic$waic, mlik = m$mlik[1, 1]
))
altitude_site <- purrr::imap_dfr(
  altitude_model, \(m, shape) mutate(site_probability(m), shape = shape, species = "Gobio gobio")
)
rm(altitude_model)
```

We plot predicted minus observed presence of the gudgeon models with a linear
and with a quadratic log altitude averaged over the visits in hexagons.

```{r altitude-shape-map}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.5

altitude_site |>
  mutate(
    species = factor(species, map_species),
    shape = factor(paste(shape, "altitude"), c("linear altitude", "quadratic altitude"))
  ) |>
  residual_hexagon(shape) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = residual), color = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = sf::st_transform(basin_kept, 2154), fill = NA, color = "grey40") +
  facet_wrap(~shape) +
  residual_scale +
  theme_void() +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 11))
```

We extract model WAIC and likelihood to compare their performance.

```{r altitude-shape-fit}
altitude_fit |>
  mutate(
    waic_vs_quadratic = round(waic - waic[shape == "quadratic"], 1),
    mlik_vs_quadratic = round(mlik - mlik[shape == "quadratic"], 1)
  ) |>
  select(shape, dam_effect, waic_vs_quadratic, mlik_vs_quadratic) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

For the gudgeon, the model with quadratic altitude is clearly better (lower
WAIC, larger likelihood). The map of residuals tells us where it performs
better. The linear model over-predicts gudgeons in the uplands (Massif Central
and Pyrenees), while the quadratic model remove this excess. We then decide to
keep the quadratic altitude term for all species, to account for such trends
that could otherwise bias the dams term.

```{r presence-models}
# Presence models of all the species found at >= 30 sites (targets
# `dam_presence_species`, `presence_model`), with the controls of the
# target `presence_term`, and the same models without the spatial field
# (target `presence_model_nofield`).
presence_model <- tar_read(presence_model)

species_group <- presence |>
  distinct(species = species_valid) |>
  left_join(tar_read(species_traits) |> select(species, is_native), by = "species") |>
  mutate(group = case_when(
    species %in% migratory ~ "migratory",
    !is_native ~ "non-native",
    .default = "native resident"
  ))

# Posterior mean and 95% credible interval of the dam effect of `model`.
dam_effect <- function(model) {
  effect <- model$summary.fixed["accumulation", ]
  tibble(
    species = model$species,
    estimate = effect$mean, lower = effect$`0.025quant`, upper = effect$`0.975quant`
  )
}
presence_effect <- bind_rows(
  `with spatial field` = purrr::map_dfr(presence_model, dam_effect),
  `without spatial field` = purrr::map_dfr(tar_read(presence_model_nofield), dam_effect),
  .id = "model"
) |>
  left_join(species_group |> select(species, group), by = "species") |>
  # Imprecise: 95% interval of the main model wider than 2 logit units.
  mutate(
    imprecise = any(model == "with spatial field" & upper - lower > 2),
    .by = species
  )
```

Effect of the dams on the presence of each species, with (main model) and
without the spatial field. 
We separate species whose inference is imprecise, this is due to poor sampling,
and in particular indicates little site with a dam downstream have been sampled.

```{r presence-models-plot}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: !expr 2 + 0.25 * length(tar_read(dam_presence_species))

group_color <- c(
  migratory = "#B2182B", `non-native` = "#E69F00", `native resident` = "grey40"
)
species_order <- presence_effect |>
  filter(model == "with spatial field") |>
  arrange(desc(estimate)) |>
  pull(species)
presence_effect |>
  mutate(
    species = factor(species, species_order),
    panel = if_else(imprecise, "imprecise", "precise") |> factor(c("precise", "imprecise"))
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(estimate, species, color = group, shape = model)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(
    aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper), size = 0.3,
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.6)
  ) +
  facet_grid(panel ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y") +
  scale_color_manual(values = group_color) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(`with spatial field` = 16, `without spatial field` = 1)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-3, 2)) +
  labs(x = "Effect of log(1 + large dams downstream)", y = NULL, color = NULL, shape = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(face = "italic"), legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 2), shape = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
```

With the spatial field 6 species are credibly found less frequently upstream of
dams:

- Eel (*Anguilla anguilla*)
- Wels catfish (*Silurus glanis*)
- Ruffe (*Gymnocephalus cernua*)
- Sander (*Sander luciopera*)
- Blicca (*Blicca bjoerkna*)
- Stone moroko (*Pseudorasbora parva*)

We find the obvious anadromous eel, as well as species that can live in brackish
waters (Blicca, Sander, Ruffe, Stone moroko), and the invasive wels catfish.
This suggest that dams block upstream colonisation of brackish species and the
colonisation of new areas by the wels.

Below, we analyse the spatial fields for each species, to look for patterns that
we may have missed.

### Patterns shared by the spatial fields

The spatial field of each species takes up what the covariates miss at the scale
of tens to hundreds of kilometres. If several species share the same pattern, it
might suggest that something regional that the covariates do not capture
(climate, geology, colonisation history, other stressors) acts on all of them.
To find these shared patterns, we compute the field of each species at the sites
and run a PCA.

```{r field-pca}
site <- distinct(visit, sandre_code, .keep_all = TRUE)
site_A <- INLA::inla.spde.make.A(spatial_mesh, loc = visit_coordinates(site))
field_site <- sapply(presence_model, \(model) as.vector(site_A %*% model$summary.random$spatial$mean))
colnames(field_site) <- sapply(presence_model, `[[`, "species")
field_pca <- prcomp(field_site, scale. = TRUE)
round(summary(field_pca)$importance[2, 1:5], 2)

field_score <- site |>
  select(sandre_code, longitude, latitude, district, dams, log_alt, log_dist, log_width, log_slope) |>
  bind_cols(as_tibble(field_pca$x[, 1:2]))
field_loading <- as_tibble(field_pca$rotation[, 1:2], rownames = "species") |>
  left_join(species_group |> select(species, group), by = "species")
```

Score of each site on the first two axes.

```{r field-pca-map}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.5

field_score |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(PC1, PC2), names_to = "axis", values_to = "score") |>
  ggplot(aes(longitude, latitude)) +
  geom_sf(
    data = sf::st_transform(basin_kept, 4326), fill = "grey97",
    color = "grey40", inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_point(aes(color = score), size = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~axis) +
  scale_color_distiller(palette = "PuOr", direction = 1, name = "Score") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 11))
```

Loading of each species on the first two axes.

```{r field-pca-loading}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 7

ggplot(field_loading, aes(PC1, PC2, color = group)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey70") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey70") +
  geom_point() +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = species), size = 2.7, fontface = "italic", max.overlaps = 40, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = group_color) +
  labs(color = NULL)
```

Correlation of the site scores with the dam count and the position
covariates.

```{r field-pca-covariates}
field_score |>
  transmute(PC1, PC2, accumulation = log1p(dams), log_alt, log_dist, log_width, log_slope) |>
  cor() |>
  (\(x) x[c("PC1", "PC2"), -(1:2)])() |>
  round(2) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

The Brittany axis points to something regional that the position covariates
miss. The first axis may reflect water temperature: the species with high
loadings are cold-water species, those with low loadings warm-water ones. We
compare the site scores with the mean July air temperature of the river reach
(RHT, 1960-1990).

```{r field-pca-temperature}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4.5

field_temperature <- field_score |>
  left_join(
    site |> select(sandre_code, operation_id),
    by = "sandre_code"
  ) |>
  left_join(
    tar_read(inland_operations_rht) |>
      sf::st_drop_geometry() |>
      select(operation_id, july_temperature = tjuil_moy),
    by = "operation_id"
  )
temperature_cor <- with(field_temperature, cor(PC1, july_temperature, use = "complete.obs"))

ggplot(field_temperature, aes(july_temperature, PC1)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.6, alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, color = "#B2182B") +
  labs(
    x = "Mean July air temperature (°C)", y = "Site score on PC1",
    subtitle = paste("Correlation:", round(temperature_cor, 2))
  )
```

The hypothesis that most spatial field capture a water effect is supported by
the correlation between PC1 and July air temperature.
